title: Hands Together
passage:
The clapping in the school hall starts a beat before the recorder has stopped, and it starts everywhere at once. That is the part worth noticing. No one has agreed to anything, there is no conductor to watch, and yet two hundred people find the same half-second. ___(1)___, the ending is unanimous: five seconds later the sound stops, and again there has been no signal.

Somebody has to be first, though, and first is the exposed position. The risk of putting your hands together in a quiet room is that the room may not ___(2)___ in, and for the length of one clap you are alone with an opinion nobody asked for. That is why the second pair of hands matters more than the first: it turns a private view into a public event. A hall organises itself in about a fifth of a second, and not one of the people in it could explain how.

Ending is the harder half. Nobody wants to be the last pair of hands still going, so the sound comes down faster than it went up, and the coming-down is a ___(3)___ about how long is decent, conducted at speed and without words. Although what a hall gives an eight-year-old is ___(4)___, it is not permitted to run long. Four or five seconds, then a ragged tail from the two or three people who were slow, then the scrape of a chair. The tail is the seam, and every hall has one.

The mechanism shows itself when it slips. Two people begin at the wrong pause in a concerto and stop as though scalded. A room asked for a big hand for a stranger will give one ___(5)___, and everybody present can hear that it is not the same sound the recorder got. Then there is the clapping that will not stop, at a leaving do or after bad news, where the usual length is refused on purpose, and the refusal is the message. At the end of the summer concert a boy in the second row went on clapping long after the hall had finished, watching the stage, entirely unembarrassed, until his mother put a hand on his arm.
– Hilary Dempsey

questions.rationale: The word that fits is Equally (C). The sentence before it reports one surprising thing, that two hundred people find the same half-second with nobody having agreed to anything, and this sentence reports a second thing of the same kind at the other end of the burst, marking it as independent with “and again there has been no signal”. The relation is parallel addition, and Equally is the single word here that supplies it. Hence would claim a consequence, but a room finding the start together does not cause it to find the stop together, and the clause insists that the second feat is unsignalled in its own right. Rather withdraws or corrects something just said, and nothing in the previous sentence is being taken back. Elsewhere sends a reader to a different place, and the paragraph never leaves this one hall. All four are single-word sentence openers followed by a comma, so word class decides nothing and the discourse relation between the two sentences has to be read.

The word that fits is join (A). The sentence sets out the danger of clapping first: that the other hands in the hall do not come in behind you. To join in is the ordinary English way of saying that somebody starts taking part in what other people are doing, and no other word on this list means that. To fall in is to form up in ranks, a marching sense with no social use in a school hall. To break in is to interrupt a person who is already speaking, or to enter a building by force; this room is not interrupting anything, it is failing to start. To cut in is to push into a conversation, a queue or a dance, an interruption again and not a joining. Every option is a bare verb after “may not” and every option makes a real phrasal verb with in, so only the sense can decide, and the clause that follows – “you are alone with an opinion nobody asked for” – says which sense is wanted.

The word that fits is negotiation (B). The clause says the end of the applause is worked out between people, at speed and without words, and it hangs the noun on “about how long is decent”. A negotiation names a process still under way, and of these four nouns it is the one that takes an about-phrase comfortably. A transaction is a completed piece of business, normally with a payment on one side of it, and people do not conduct one about a question. A bargain is the terms two sides have already struck, so it names an outcome and not a working-out, and English pairs it with someone or over something. A settlement is what closes a dispute, which is the far end of the process from the one being described. The options are singular abstract nouns from the same commercial and social stock, so what separates them is the stage each one names and the preposition each one takes.

The word that fits is wholehearted (D). The clause opens with “Although”, so the adjective has to stand in real tension with what comes after it, and what comes after is that the applause is not permitted to run long. Only a word at the warm end of the scale makes that tension: a hall that gives a child something wholehearted and then stops it after five seconds really is doing two things at once. Grudging and muted both fail, and they fail in the same way. Applause that is reluctant, or applause that is subdued, is applause you would expect to be short, so the concession word at the front of the sentence would have nothing left to mark. Outspoken fails on another axis. It is a real adjective at the forceful end, but English applies it to people and to the views they voice, not to the noise a room makes with its hands.

The word that fits is dutifully (B). This room has been asked for its applause and supplies it on cue, and the sentence turns on the sound being thinner than the one that came unprompted, which it states outright: “it is not the same sound the recorder got”. Dutifully carries exactly that, something done because it is owed and not because it is felt. Generously runs against the sentence, because a generous response would be the same sound or a warmer one, and the sentence denies that. Instinctively is the tempting wrong answer, since the piece elsewhere is about clapping that nobody organises; but this room was asked, and a response to a request is the one thing an instinct cannot be. Narrowly is a real adverb that keeps narrow company – a narrowly avoided accident, a narrowly won vote – and it tells a reader nothing about the manner in which a sound is produced. Four adverbs in -ly stand in one slot, so the sense is again the whole of the discrimination.

(c) MOVE SEQUENCE: a scene and the thing in it worth noticing -> the exposed position of going first -> the second pair of hands as the real hinge -> the harder half, ending, and what its ragged tail shows -> three failure cases -> a boy who does not stop. No skeptic slot, no objection paragraph, no verdict sentence. (d) OPENINGS: not the received-explanation template that RULE 24 bars for every batch22 unit, and not a definition or a date.
